title: MethodX under stochastic execution delays (plain plan)
method: MethodX wraps a sample-efficient model-based agent with a learned latent world model (representation H, latent dynamics G, reward/value/policy heads, MCTS) for MDPs with exogenous, observed execution delays z_t ≤ M. It keeps queues of the last M prescribed actions and their observed delays; a pending-queue resolver computes the actions that will actually execute over the next z_t steps from effective decision times; it applies G z_t times from H(o_t) to predict the latent state at execution time and runs MCTS there; the first M actions are planned from s_0 by alternating policy and dynamics; after each episode, replay stores the executed action a_{τ_t} instead of the decided one; the policy loss targets the MCTS distribution at the predicted state. Only acting, episode post-processing and evaluation change.

compute.hardware: 2x RTX 2080 Ti-class GPUs per training run, ~1 day per run

claims.text: A formalism that separates the delay process from the MDP, with no state augmentation
Markov policies suffice when delays are observed
Higher return under constant, stochastic and large delays, with sample efficiency retained

questions.text: E0: is the shared delay wrapper correct (τ_t, overwrites, duplicates, default queue) and does the pending-queue resolver predict the actions that actually execute?
questions.hypothesis: The wrapper matches hand-worked traces and is the identity for M = 0 or z ≡ 0; the resolver's predicted actions equal the executed actions over 10^6 random steps for each delay distribution

questions.text: E1: on small tabular MDPs, does the non-stationary Markov policy class reach the augmented-state optimum, and how much does MethodX's point-prediction policy lose?
questions.hypothesis: V*_aug equals the optimum of the non-stationary Markov class up to numerical error under constant and stochastic delays; the oblivious policy is strictly worse; the augmented state grows as |S||A|^M while the formalism's does not

questions.text: E2: under constant delay (M ∈ {5, 15, 25}, deterministic dynamics), does MethodX get higher return than the oblivious, augmented, Delayed-Q and augmentation-based random-delay baselines?
E3: under stochastic delays (i.i.d. uniform, random walk, heavy-tailed; M ∈ {5, 15, 25}), and with sticky actions, does MethodX get higher return than the baselines?
E3 distribution shift: trained under i.i.d. uniform delays and evaluated under random-walk and heavy-tailed delays (and the reverse), how much does MethodX degrade?
questions.hypothesis: MethodX degrades little, because it only consumes the observed z_t

questions.text: E4: does wrapping another model-based tree-search learner (MuZero or Gumbel MuZero) improve it over its oblivious version?
E5: which modifications account for the gains, and does observing z matter?
questions.hypothesis: The planned initial queue matters most at large M and on short episodes; storing the decided a_t instead of the executed action causes a large drop, since the model learns wrong dynamics

questions.text: E6: does MethodX retain the backbone's sample efficiency, and where does the learned model fail at large M?
questions.hypothesis: MethodX's learning curve has a similar shape to the delay-free backbone's and its retention ratio stays high throughout training, not only at 100k

stochastic heavy-tailed: mostly small delays with rare spikes to M
